info.title: Skyward Control Plane
info.description:
Two families of resource.

**Declarative** (`compute`, `node`) carry `spec` (intent) and `status` (observation). `PATCH` only touches `spec`; `status` is written by the reconciler. There is no `operation` resource — `generation` vs `status.observed_generation` is the progress.

**Imperative** (`task`) are append-only facts with one terminal outcome. `executions` are the physical attempts; retrying creates an execution, never a task, so a `Future` keeps a stable handle.

put.description:
A compute has at most one live owner per generation; zero is legitimate and temporary (daemon restarting, script killed).

Claiming requires the current lease to be expired or absent — it is a CAS. Renewing requires being the current owner. Losing renewals destroys nothing by itself: if `spec.delete_on_exit` is `true`, reconciliation tears the compute down; if `false`, it simply sits ownerless until something adopts it.

Idempotent by `Idempotency-Key`: the same key with the same payload returns the original resource with `200`; with a different payload, `409 idempotency_conflict`.

Does not wait for readiness — returns `status.state: requested` and the client observes the resource or the event stream. There is no `operation` resource: `generation` vs `status.observed_generation` is the progress.

post.summary: Create a generation (apply drift, or roll back)
post.description:
Replacing infrastructure *is* creating a new generation: quiesce, drain, destroy the old one, provision the new one — same `compute_id`.

Without `source`, applies the drift pending in `status.drift`. With `source`, rolls back to that generation.

`force: true` marks unresolved tasks as `indeterminate` before replacing; `force: false` refuses while executions are still active.

delete.description:
Writes `spec.desired: deleted`. Not synchronous, and not a detach: reconciliation continues until the provider **confirms the resources are gone**, and only then does `status.state` become `deleted`.

No process shutdown ever issues this command.

patch.description:
Only `spec.nodes` is mutable in place: it bumps `generation` and the reconciler resizes with drain.

Changing immutable fields (provider, image, worker, plugins, volumes, ports) is **drift**: it is recorded in `status.drift`, the applied definition is kept, and no infrastructure is replaced. Replacing requires `POST /computes/{id}/generations`.

delete.description:
Nodes are not directly creatable — they come from reconciling `spec.nodes`. But a node can be condemned: `desired: deleted` blocks new assignments, waits for the executions it is known to hold, then destroys the instance.

If the compute still wants that capacity, the reconciler creates **another** node for the same `rank`, with a new `id`. The old node's tombstone remains.

get.description: Includes tombstones by default. A node that died stays listed, with its `provider_binding` intact, until the provider confirms termination — that is what stops an instance from going missing with nobody knowing.

put.description:
The body is the binary envelope (cloudpickle + compression). The server recomputes the hash over the serialized bytes before compression and rejects with `hash_mismatch` if it disagrees with the path.

Accepting cloudpickle is accepting arbitrary code execution. In local single-user mode that is explicit: the caller is the user themselves.

delete.description: Before `started`, cancellation is guaranteed (CAS + worker ack). After `started` it is best-effort: the execution enters `cancel_requested` and only becomes `cancelled` once the worker confirms it stopped. Without that confirmation the outcome is `indeterminate` — Python code that may still be running is never declared cancelled.

post.description:
Retrying **is** creating another physical attempt of the same task — the `task_id` stays the user's handle. The new execution points `retry_of` at the previous one.

Retrying an `indeterminate` outcome requires `acknowledge_duplication: true`: the system does not know whether the previous execution had side effects, and will not pretend it does.

post.description:
A task is **one call**: `function` + `args` → `result`. It is what the SDK's `Future[T]` points at, and its `id` survives retries and SDK restarts.

`dispatch: one` (the `>>` operator) creates a single execution. `dispatch: all` (the `@` operator) freezes the set of `ready` nodes at admission and creates one execution per rank — a later scale-up does not add executions.

The task and its first execution are persisted **before** any dispatch to a worker. The worker dedupes on `(task_id, execution_id, args_hash)`.

400.description: Bad request syntax or unsupported method

get.description:
The result survives controller and SDK restarts, and reading does not consume it — only an explicit purge removes it.

`204` means there is no terminal outcome yet. A non-successful terminal outcome answers `409` with the error code (`task_failed`, `task_indeterminate`, ...).

400.description: Bad request syntax or unsupported method

get.description:
For a task submitted with `dispatch: stream` — a generator on the far side. **This request is the dispatch**: nothing starts a streaming task on its own, because the only process that can hold the far end of a stream is the one consuming it.

Length-prefixed msgpack frames: 4 bytes big-endian, then the frame. A frame is an item or a failure, and a failure is the last one — by the time a generator raises, the caller already has the items before it, and there is no status code left to fail with.

Not resumable. A dropped stream is a dead stream; submit another task.

400.description: Bad request syntax or unsupported method

get.description:
Each event's `id:` is the **global sequence**, monotonic. `Last-Event-ID` replays from the event log; the snapshot and the cursor are captured in the same logical order, so there is no gap between reading state and subscribing.

There is no automatic event GC, so any valid cursor stays resumable.

A slow consumer never blocks a commit: the adapter closes the connection when its local queue overflows and the client reconnects from its last id.

Task stdout/stderr and node bootstrap output are events here. There is no `logs` resource with a second source of truth.

400.description: Bad request syntax or unsupported method

post.description:
A provider is a named account, not a kind: two AWS accounts, two Vast keys and two regions can coexist, and a compute refers to the provider it wants by id or name.

Credentials are validated against the kind's `credential_fields` before the row is written, and are never returned by any read path.

get.summary: List the provider kinds this build supports
get.description: Capability negotiation happens here, before anything is created: each kind declares the credentials it needs and how long its offers stay fresh. A kind absent from this list cannot be registered.

Served from the cache. Any provider whose offers have expired is refreshed first — the TTL belongs to the provider, because a marketplace bundle is gone in minutes while a fixed instance type is not.

A refresh that fails does not empty the catalog: the stale rows are still served and the failure shows up as `last_error` on the provider. A provider being down degrades the answer; it does not erase it.
